title: AI Is Reshaping Cybersecurity Faster Than Defenses Can Keep Up
excerpt: As AI accelerates both vulnerability discovery and exploitation, security teams face a shrinking window to adapt — with experts warning that weaponisation of software flaws now takes hours, not weeks.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Mozilla's AI model found 271 vulnerabilities in Firefox, surpassing traditional monthly findings.
  • CrowdStrike warns AI could exponentially increase zero-day vulnerabilities, reducing exploitation time to hours.
  • AI-generated reports overwhelmed open-source maintainers, prompting new submission rules in May 2026.
  • Organizations must shift to autonomous remediation as AI enables exploits for under $50.

  • Mozilla used a frontier AI model to uncover and patch 271 Firefox vulnerabilities in a single release — far exceeding what traditional tools found monthly over the prior year.
  • CrowdStrike's president warns AI could trigger exponential growth in zero-day vulnerabilities, with exploitation timelines collapsing from weeks to hours.
  • AI-generated vulnerability reports have already overwhelmed open-source maintainers, forcing the Linux kernel team to update submission rules in May 2026.
  • Security industry leaders say organisations must shift from manual patching to autonomous remediation as AI enables attackers to build working exploits for under $50.

The Bug-Finding Machine

For decades, cybersecurity researchers discovered software vulnerabilities the same way: automated tools found bugs, and humans decided which ones mattered. That division of labour is collapsing.

In a commentary published in Nature on July 16, Thorsten Holz, scientific director at the Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy in Bochum, Germany, described how AI systems now go far beyond code generation. Modern models can triage software crashes, identify root causes, assess exploitability, and propose fixes — tasks that once required years of specialist experience.

The results are already measurable. Earlier in 2026, Mozilla deployed a frontier AI model to audit its Firefox browser and uncovered 271 vulnerabilities in a single version release, according to Holz. That figure exceeded what the company's existing tools and human reviewers had found each month over the previous year.

A Flood of Zero-Days

The defensive gains come with a mirror-image threat. Mike Sentonas, president of CrowdStrike, told Fast Company that more than 100 new vulnerabilities are publicly disclosed on an average day — and AI is poised to multiply that number dramatically.

"Theoretically, we all wake up and there is just an exponential growth in zero-day vulnerabilities, and there are no patches."

- Mike Sentonas, President, CrowdStrike

Sentonas warned that frontier AI will "drastically reduce the time between a flaw existing and somebody discovering how to exploit it." Banks, hospitals, factories, and utilities — organisations reliant on legacy hardware that cannot be quickly upgraded — face the earliest exposure.

The problem extends beyond vulnerability discovery. AI agents introduce entirely new attack surfaces: credential theft, memory poisoning, agent-to-agent abuse, and runtime manipulation, Sentonas said. Security policies written for one model can become obsolete before they clear an approval process.

Hours, Not Weeks

Anthropic's recent Mythos model disclosure sharpened the urgency. James Greenwood, AVP Solutions Engineering for Asia-Pacific at Tanium, said the findings confirmed what many in the industry feared.

"The window from CVE disclosure to weaponisation is now measured in hours, not days, and certainly not the weeks businesses have planned around. AI is already building working exploits from known vulnerabilities in hours for under US$50."

- James Greenwood, AVP Solutions Engineering APAC, Tanium

Greenwood argued that organisations must move from manual reaction to autonomous control — routine patching, compliance validation, and vulnerability closure happening at machine speed, with humans setting policy and reviewing exceptions.

Open-Source Under Pressure

The shift is already straining the infrastructure that underpins much of the internet. In May 2026, the Linux kernel maintenance team responded to a surge of duplicate AI-assisted vulnerability reports by issuing new submission guidelines. The problem, Holz wrote, was not that maintainers were failing — it was that machine-generated reports overwhelmed processes built for human-speed discovery.

With open-source AI models rapidly approaching the capabilities of closed frontier systems, the tools to find and exploit vulnerabilities are becoming broadly accessible. Attackers no longer need to build advanced systems from scratch.

What Comes Next

For India's large cybersecurity workforce — which staffs security operations centres for global banks, tech firms, and consulting giants — the transformation is both a professional opportunity and an operational challenge. Indian IT services companies managing security for Fortune 500 clients will need to retool their teams for AI-augmented threat hunting and autonomous remediation, even as the volume of AI-generated threats rises.

Sentonas urged security teams to map their organisations' AI usage, limit access rights, and scan their own code now. "The complexity of the world we're living in is going to change dramatically every month," he said.

The consensus among researchers and industry leaders is clear: the window to prepare is narrow, and the cost of delay is measured in breaches.
